16:1.text: And I heard another out of the altar say, Even so, Lord God Almighty, true and righteous are thy judgments.

provenance.route: Revelation 16:7 and Romans 14:11 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “righteous are thy judgments” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “confess to God” occurs in exactly one; the two are Revelation 16:7 and Romans 14:11.
provenance.alternative: Revelation 19:2 has “true and righteous are his judgments” in the third person, which is Mosiah 16:1's person; and Revelation 15:4, “for thy judgments are made manifest”, is the verse that pairs the vindication of God's judgments with all nations coming to worship.
provenance.significance: Abinadi's last sentence is built out of the two KJV verses in which a creature acknowledges that God's judgments are right, and it puts the acknowledgement in the mouth of the audience formula he used at 15:28. Romans 14:11 supplies the confessing — every tongue shall confess to God, which Paul is quoting from Isaiah 45:23 as proof that all shall stand before the judgment seat — and Revelation 16:7 supplies what is confessed, that the judgments are righteous, spoken from under the altar after the third vial. Both are universal-acknowledgement verses and both concern a judgment already executed. What the Book of Mormon adds is the sight: the nations do not merely confess, they see eye to eye, which is Isaiah 52:8's phrase from the verse Abinadi transcribed twelve verses earlier.

16:1.note: “Every nation, kindred, tongue and people, shall see eye to eye, and shall confess before God that his judgments are just.” Three KJV strands in one clause, two of them singletons. The nation-formula is Revelation 14:6's, adjudicated at 15:28; “see eye to eye” is Isaiah 52:8's, transcribed at 15:29; and the confession is Romans 14:11's with Revelation 16:7's object. Recorded at moderate because none of the three is reproduced at length and the sentence is a compound of formulas Abinadi has already used — which is itself the finding, since 16:1 is the peroration and is assembled from the chapter he has just finished.

16:1.text: And Moses said unto the people, Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will shew to you to day: for the Egyptians whom ye have seen to day, ye shall see them again no more for ever.

provenance.other: “See the salvation of the Lord” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 14:13 and 2 Chronicles 20:17, and both are a commander telling a terrified people to stand still and watch God fight. Isaiah 52:10, which Mosiah 15:31 has just transcribed, reads “the salvation of our God”.
provenance.significance: This is a small mediation finding and worth having. Mosiah 15:31 ends the previous chapter with Isaiah 52:10 verbatim — “all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God” — and one verse later Abinadi says it again in his own voice as “all shall see the salvation of the Lord”, which is not Isaiah's phrase but Exodus 14:13's. The switch is from the possessive to the divine name, and it moves the sentence from a prophecy about the nations to the formula Moses uses at the Red Sea and Jehoshaphat uses before a battle: stand still and see. Abinadi has spent two chapters as Moses (13:5) and is about to be killed; the last thing he tells his judges to expect is the sight Israel was told to expect when the sea opened.

16:1.note: “The time shall come when all shall see the salvation of the Lord.” Two KJV verses have the phrase and both are eve-of-deliverance speeches to a people who are about to watch rather than act. The interest is in the departure from the immediately preceding verse: Isaiah 52:10 at Mosiah 15:31 reads “the salvation of our God”, and Abinadi's own restatement one verse later takes the other KJV form. Recorded at moderate — five common words — but the substitution is real and it is visible only because the two verses are adjacent.

16:2.text: And shall cast them into a furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth.

provenance.other: “Wailing and gnashing of teeth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 13:42 and 13:50, both of the furnace of fire; the commoner “weeping and gnashing of teeth” is Matthew's elsewhere and Luke's. “Weep and howl” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Joel 1:5 and James 5:1.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon's list has four verbs where the KJV never has more than two, and it has taken one pair from each of the KJV's two formulas — “weep” and “gnash” from the Matthean furnace sayings, “howl” and “wail” from the prophetic and Jacobean woe-oracles. The result is a compound that exists in no verse and reads as though it existed in all of them. Note where Abinadi is standing when he says it: he has just been condemned by a king who will burn him (17:20), and the KJV's home for “wailing and gnashing of teeth” is a furnace of fire.

16:2.note: “They shall have cause to howl, and weep, and wail, and gnash their teeth.” A four-verb fusion of the KJV's two damnation formulas, neither reproduced whole. Recorded at moderate for that reason — no single verse is the source — and kept because every one of the four verbs is a KJV eschatological verb and the collocation of gnashing with weeping is Matthew's alone. The Book of Mormon's addition is the causal frame, “shall have cause to”, which converts a description of hell into a verdict about desert.

16:3.text: And the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world: he was cast out into the earth, and his angels were cast out with him.

provenance.route: Revelation 12:9 and 2 Corinthians 11:3 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “That old serpent” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 12:9 and 20:2, and both identify him as the Devil and Satan. “Beguiled Eve” occurs in exactly one, 2 Corinthians 11:3.
provenance.significance: Genesis never says the serpent of Eden was the devil. The identification is made in the KJV only in Revelation 12:9 and 20:2 — “that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan” — and the connection to Eden specifically is made only by Paul, who says the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty. Mosiah 16:3 asserts the whole doctrine in one clause and does it in the two sources' own words: “that old serpent that did beguile our first parents”. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Genesis 3:1-24 at this verse, which is where the story is; the wording is from the two New Testament passages that interpret it, and the catalogue puts the link where the wording is (CONVENTIONS §6a).

16:3.note: “Yea, even that old serpent that did beguile our first parents, which was the cause of their fall.” Two KJV phrases in eight words, from the only verses that make the identification the sentence depends on. Paul's verb is exactly reproduced with the object generalized — “beguiled Eve” becomes “beguile our first parents”, which brings Adam into a deception the New Testament pointedly assigns to Eve alone (1 Timothy 2:14 says Adam was not deceived). That generalization is not incidental: the next clause makes the fall the cause of all mankind becoming carnal, and a fall that runs through both parents is the one that can bear that weight.

16:3.text: This wisdom descendeth not from above, but is earthly, sensual, devilish.

provenance.other: “Earthly, sensual, devilish” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The KJV uses “sensual” only twice, here and at Jude 19; “devilish” only here.
provenance.significance: The triad is James's and it is unique in the Bible — the one place the KJV puts those three adjectives in a row, describing a wisdom that does not descend from above. Mosiah 16:3 reproduces the sequence with the first term replaced: carnal, sensual, devilish. The substitution is the argument. James's “earthly” is a location, and the Book of Mormon's “carnal” is a nature, which is the word the verse has already used twice (“they are carnal and devilish”) and which lets the triad describe fallen humanity rather than a kind of counsel. The phrase becomes a fixed formula in the corpus, and this is where it enters.

16:3.note: “The cause of all mankind becoming carnal, sensual, devlish.” Two of three adjectives verbatim, in James's order, from a KJV singleton — and the 1830's spelling “devlish”, twice in this verse, is the compositor's rather than a reading, corrected in 1920. What James says of a wisdom, Abinadi says of a species. Note that the verse has already used the pair “carnal and devilish” at its opening, so the triad arrives as an expansion of Abinadi's own phrase into James's, which is why “carnal” rather than “earthly” heads it.

16:3.text: For God doth know that in the day ye eat thereof, then your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.

provenance.other: “Knowing good and evil” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 3:5, the serpent's promise; Genesis 3:22 has “to know good and evil”. Mosiah 16:3 reads “knowing evil from good”.
provenance.significance: The serpent's promise in the KJV is that eating will make them “as gods, knowing good and evil”, and it is the one verse with that participle. Mosiah 16:3 reverses the terms and adds a preposition: “knowing evil from good”. The change turns a possession into a discrimination — not knowing both, but telling one from the other — and it turns the serpent's inducement into the fall's result, since in Mosiah's sentence the knowledge stands in a list with becoming carnal and subjecting oneself to the devil. Hardy's apparatus points to Genesis 3:1-24 for the verse as a whole, and this participle is the only phrase in it that is actually Genesis's.

16:3.note: “Knowing evil from good, subjecting themselves to the devil.” The participle is Genesis 3:5's, in the KJV's only occurrence, with the nouns inverted and “from” inserted. Recorded at moderate: three words, and the inversion is the kind a writer makes without a text open. It is kept because it discharges Hardy's Genesis 3 cross-reference at the point where wording actually exists, and because the rest of the verse's language is demonstrably from Revelation 12, 2 Corinthians 11 and James 3 rather than from Genesis at all — which is the finding worth having about this verse.

16:5.text: Because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be.

provenance.other: “The carnal mind is enmity against God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The formula “the enemy of God” is James 4:4's, in the KJV's only verse making a person rather than a disposition God's enemy.
provenance.significance: Romans 8:7 is the KJV's one statement that the carnal is at enmity with God, and it gives a reason: “for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be.” Mosiah 16:5 states the same doctrine and keeps the same structure — a man who persists in his carnal nature remains fallen and is an enemy to God — and then adds a sentence Paul does not have: “and also is the devil an enemy to God.” The addition puts the carnal man and the devil in one category, which is what 16:3 has just prepared by making the fall the devil's work and its result a carnal nature. Where Paul has an incapacity, Abinadi has an allegiance.

16:5.note: “He that persists in his own carnal nature … being an enemy to God; and also is the devil an enemy to God.” No clause is reproduced, so this is proposed on the doctrine and its vocabulary: “carnal” with “enemy/enmity” and God, which the KJV brings together in exactly one verse. James 4:4 supplies the noun in the form the Book of Mormon uses, “the enemy of God”, where Paul has the abstract “enmity”. Recorded at moderate; a reader who wants a verbal source will not find one here, and the case is that both of the KJV's two ways of saying this are present in one sentence.

16:7.text: O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?

provenance.other: “O grave, where is thy victory” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The King James text pairs the two nouns in a particular way — sting with death, victory with the grave — and Mosiah 16:7 keeps both pairings intact: “that the grave should have no victory, and that death should have no sting”.
provenance.significance: This is a strong case for kjvSpecific because the pairing is a feature of the King James text rather than of the doctrine. Paul's rhetorical questions could be assigned either way round, and the Book of Mormon does not assign them either way round: it gives the grave the victory and death the sting, exactly as the KJV prints them, and in the KJV's own order of clauses reversed to put the grave first. A writer paraphrasing the doctrine of resurrection from memory would have no reason to keep the nouns attached to those particular predicates; a writer with the KJV's two questions in his ear would find it hard not to.

16:7.note: “If Christ had not risen from the dead, or have broken the bands of death, that the grave should have no victory, and that death should have no sting, there could have been no resurrection.” Paul's two questions turned into two counterfactual clauses with the noun pairings preserved. “The bands of death” is this speech's own formula (15:8, 15:9, 15:23) and has no KJV source; everything else in the sentence is 1 Corinthians 15:55-56. Note the argumentative direction: Paul's questions are a taunt after the victory, and Abinadi's clauses are conditions before it — the same words used to say what would have failed rather than what has been overcome.

16:8.text: So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory.

provenance.other: “Swallowed up in victory” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “the sting of death” occurs in exactly one; they are 1 Corinthians 15:54 and 15:56, two verses apart.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 16:8 splices the two. Paul says death is swallowed up in victory (15:54) and, after the taunt, that the sting of death is sin (15:56); the Book of Mormon says “the sting of death is swallowed up in Christ”, which takes 15:56's subject and 15:54's predicate and replaces Paul's abstract “victory” with a person. The substitution is the doctrine of the whole chapter in one word: what swallows death is not an outcome but Christ. It also completes a movement begun at 15:7, where the same verb was used of the Son's will being swallowed up in the Father's — the chapter borrows Paul's one distinctive verb twice and uses it once for the incarnation and once for the resurrection.

16:8.note: “There is a resurrection, therefore the grave hath no victory, and the sting of death is swallowed up in Christ.” Two KJV singletons two verses apart in Paul, fused into one clause with “in victory” replaced by “in Christ”. The first half of the sentence resolves 16:7's counterfactual — the grave has no victory, indicatively now — so the two verses together reproduce 1 Corinthians 15:54-56 as a hypothesis and its denial. Below any quotation threshold and catalogued as an allusion; what carries it is that both singletons appear, in Paul's order, in eighteen words.

16:9.text: In him was life; and the life was the light of men.

provenance.route: John 1:4 and John 8:12 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “In him was life” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “the life of the world” occurs in exactly one, John 6:51. “The light of the world” occurs in three, of which two are John's (8:12, 9:5) and one is Jesus saying it of his disciples (Matthew 5:14).
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon's title “the light and the life of the world” has no KJV verse behind it, and the reason is that it is a compound of three of them, all from one Gospel. John 1:4 puts life and light in one sentence and makes the first the source of the second; John 8:12 makes the light of the world a self-designation; John 6:51 supplies the genitive “of the world” with life rather than light attached. Mosiah 16:9 says all three at once, and then does what John's prologue does next: it treats darkness as the thing the light defeats — “a light that is endless, that can never be darkened” against John 1:5, “the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.”

16:9.note: “He is the light and the life of the world; yea, a light that is endless, that can never be darkened.” A Johannine title assembled from three verses, two of which contain KJV singletons. What the Book of Mormon adds is endlessness — a light that cannot be darkened, a life in which there can be no more death — which is not John's emphasis and is this speech's, since Abinadi has been arguing since 15:20 about a resurrection that ends death permanently. Frederick's monograph discusses this verse in proximity to John 1:4, 8:12 and 11:25; the index behind that (data/frederick-refs.json) records co-occurrence within his text, not a proposed source, and his argument in the book is about the Gospel of John rather than about Mosiah.
bibliography: Frederick 2016: Mosiah 16:9 co-occurs with John 1:4, 8:12 and 11:25 within a 1,500-character window (co-occurrence index, data/frederick-refs.json); he proposes no source list

16:9.text: And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.

provenance.other: “There shall be no more death” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Revelation 21:4 is the KJV's one abolition of death, and it belongs to the new heaven and new earth, after the judgment of chapter 20 that Mosiah 16:10 is about to draw on. Abinadi takes the two chapters in Revelation's order — the resurrection and the books at 16:10-11 from Revelation 20, the end of death here from Revelation 21 — but reverses them, so that the endless life comes first and the judgment after. The rearrangement matters: in Revelation the abolition of death is the reward of those who survive judgment, and in Mosiah 16:9 it is a property of the Christ who will conduct it.

16:9.note: “A life which is endless, that there can be no more death.” Five words from a KJV singleton, attached to the Johannine title in the first half of the verse. Recorded at moderate — the clause is short and the sentiment is unavoidable in any statement about endless life — and kept because the KJV says it once, and because 16:10-11 goes on to use Revelation 20's judgment scene, so the two chapters of Revelation are both in view within three verses.

16:10.text: For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.

provenance.other: “This mortal must put on immortality” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “this corruptible must put on incorruption” occurs in the same verse and is repeated at 15:54.
provenance.significance: Two things are changed and both are legible. Paul's order is corruptible then mortal; Mosiah 16:10 reverses it, mortal then corruption, which puts the resurrection of the body second and lets the sentence run on into the judgment. And Paul's “corruptible”, an adjective for the thing that is raised, becomes “corruption”, the abstract state — so the Book of Mormon has corruption putting on incorruption rather than a corruptible body doing so. This catalogue has met the verse twice before, at 2 Nephi 9:7 and Enos 1:27, and neither makes that substitution; it is peculiar to Abinadi and it fits his argument, which has been about states (fallen, carnal, redeemed) rather than about bodies since 16:4.

16:10.note: “Even this mortal shall put on immortality, and this corruption shall put on incorruption.” Twelve words from a KJV singleton with the two clauses transposed and one noun abstracted. Catalogued as a quotation on the CONVENTIONS §2 rule — below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations — because the whole of Paul's sentence is reproduced and no other verse in the Bible contains it. Paul's modal “must” becomes the prophetic “shall”, which converts a condition of resurrection into a prediction of it.

16:10.text: And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.

provenance.other: “According to their works” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, two of them Revelation 20:12 and 20:13; Revelation 20:12 is the one that also has the dead standing before God. “Whether it be good, or whether it be evil” occurs in exactly two, Ecclesiastes 12:14 and Jeremiah 42:6, and only Ecclesiastes has it of a judgment.
provenance.significance: The judgment scene is Revelation 20:12's in every part: the dead stand before God, and they are judged according to their works. Ecclesiastes 12:14 supplies the alternative that Revelation leaves implicit — God shall bring every work into judgment, whether it be good, or whether it be evil — and it is the KJV's one verse pairing that formula with judgment. The Book of Mormon's own contribution is the furniture: “the bar of God”, a phrase in no KJV verse, which imports a nineteenth-century courtroom into an apocalyptic throne scene and which becomes standard in the corpus after this. Recover Revelation 20 and 16:11's two resurrections follow, since the books of Revelation 20:12 are what sorts them.

16:10.note: “Shall be brought to stand before the bar of God, to be judged of him according to their works, whether they be good or whether they be evil.” Two KJV formulas end to end, Revelation's and Ecclesiastes's, joined by a phrase that is in neither. The 1830's “whether they be good or whether they be evil” follows Ecclesiastes's construction exactly while changing the pronoun from the works to the persons — Ecclesiastes judges every work, Abinadi judges the people by them — and 16:11 then divides them by John 5:29's two resurrections.

16:11.text: And shall come forth; they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation.

provenance.other: “The resurrection of life” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “the resurrection of damnation” occurs in exactly one, and it is the same verse: John 5:29.
provenance.significance: One verse of the KJV divides the resurrection in two and names both halves, and Mosiah 16:11 reproduces the division, the two names and the criterion. John: “they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation.” Mosiah: “If they be good, to the resurrection of endless life and happiness, and if they be evil, to the resurrection of endless damnation.” The insertion is “endless”, twice, which is the word this chapter has been pressing since 16:4's “endlessly lost” and 16:9's endless light and life. John's two resurrections are outcomes; Abinadi's are durations, and the whole speech is an argument that what the law of Moses could not do was make anything last.

16:11.note: “To the resurrection of endless life and happiness … to the resurrection of endless damnation.” Both of the KJV's two names for the two resurrections come from one verse, each occurring in exactly one KJV verse, and the Book of Mormon has both with the same conditional structure and the same criterion of good and evil deeds. It is the second Johannine borrowing in three verses (see 16:9) and the second half of the judgment scene begun at 16:10 from Revelation 20:12 — the books determine the works, John's verse determines what the works are worth.

16:12.text: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!

provenance.other: “And ye would not” occurs in exactly five KJV verses; the two that follow an offer of gathering are Matthew 23:37 and Luke 13:34, its Lucan double. “The arms of mercy” occurs in no KJV verse.
provenance.alternative: The refusal formula is Deuteronomic (Deuteronomy 1:43, Isaiah 30:15) and Judges 2:17's “and yet they would not hearken” is closer to Mosiah's actual words; nothing here requires the lament over Jerusalem.
provenance.significance: The lament over Jerusalem is the KJV's one scene of arms opened and refused — how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not — and Mosiah 16:12 is the same gesture with the image changed: the arms of mercy extended, twice, and twice “they would not”. The doubling is Abinadi's own and it is what makes the case, since Matthew's clause is a single refusal and the Book of Mormon's is a refrain. Note that the corpus will eventually make the borrowing explicit at 3 Nephi 10:5, where the hen and the chickens appear; here only the gesture and the refusal are present.

16:12.note: “Having never called upon the Lord while the arms of mercy was extended towards them; for the arms of mercy was extended towards them, and they would not.” Recorded as an echo. The words “and they would not” are common enough that they identify nothing on their own; what is proposed is the scene — an offer made repeatedly by an outstretched embrace and declined — for which the KJV has one home. The 1830's singular verb under a plural subject, “the arms of mercy was extended”, twice, was corrected to “were” in 1920.
16:12.whyNot: No distinctive wording whatever. “Arms of mercy” is not in the KJV, the refusal formula is in five verses and is commonest in Deuteronomy and Isaiah, and Judges 2:17 — which the n-gram stream ranks first here — is verbally nearer than Matthew. The case rests entirely on the gesture, and a reader who declines it loses a resonance and no evidence.
